body:
Contrary to Gecko, Blink doesn't have a special path for system event listeners: events are only received if they are not blocked. that means that we can't simply run the UA event handling when `stopPropagation` is called by the content. In the Media team, we are trying to rely more heavily on the web platform events and that caused us troubles. That also means that unless we change Blink's architecture to have special treatment for system event handlers, we can't implement the change you are suggesting.

As a side note, I see that you did not mention `stopImmediatePropagation`. Did you find the problem to be different in that case or is this an oversight? We've found this method to be particularly horrible in our case because we can't work around it by simply listening to the event on the target, we have to make sure to be the first event listener. As a result, we've been looking at its usage which is fairly low at the moment (0.003% of page load) though I'm not sure if the metric made it to Stable yet.

But Blink is doing X with 'select' for example (default handling is after normal dispatch) but Y (event handling during dispatch) with 'video'. Seems like it is exposing the implementation detail of some elements to the web: is it possibly that elements using shadom dom internally have this web-exposed behavior but other types of implementation doesn't have?
Why 'video' and such aren't using default handling, similarly to 'a' (if one doesn't want to add system group) etc ?

stopImmediatePropagation() vs. stopPropagation() is not really relevant here, assuming the event handling happens inside the "UA's shadow DOM", also it isn't relevant in the case if the engine has separate group for system event listeners.
(group is wrong word here, since it is really separate capture/target/bubble phases for system listeners, but old DOM3 events spec happened to talk about groups around 15 years ago)
